modules.title: Domain 1: NLP Concepts, Morphology & Attention
modules.summary: Foundational NLP definitions, linguistic hierarchy, morpheme classification, derivation vs. inflection, the closure principle, incorporation, clitics, compounding, Kankanaey affixes, POS tagging approaches, Tagalog tagsets (Rabo 59, Buban 65, PTPOST), evaluation metrics, and the foundational Transformer architecture ('Attention Is All You Need').

sections.title: 1.1 What is NLP & Levels of Linguistic Analysis
sections.simple: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is AI that enables computers to read, analyze, and generate human language. It analyzes language across distinct hierarchical levels: speech sounds (Phonology), word construction (Morphology), vocabulary units (Lexical), grammar & parse trees (Syntactic), literal meanings (Semantic), conversational flow (Discourse), and real-world intent/context (Pragmatic).
sections.deepDive:
Academic Definition: NLP bridges computer science, artificial intelligence, and formal linguistics (Khurana et al., 2018).

The 7 Levels of Linguistic Analysis:
  1. Phonology: The sound system and phonemes of a spoken language.
  2. Morphology: Word structures, roots, and meaningful sub-components (morphemes).
  3. Lexical Level: Individual dictionary units (lexemes) and vocabulary properties.
  4. Syntactic Level: Grammatical structures, phrase hierarchies, and parse trees that govern valid sentence formation.
  5. Semantic Level: The literal, compositional meaning of words and propositions.
  6. Discourse Level: Meaning spanning multiple consecutive sentences (e.g., anaphoric references, conversational turns).
  7. Pragmatic Level: Meaning conditioned on real-world context, speaker intent, and non-literal speech acts.
Modern Paradigm: Classical rule-based techniques are now augmented with transformers and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground model responses in validated corpora.

sections.title: 1.2 Core NLP Tasks & Pipeline
sections.simple: NLP solves problems through dedicated modular tasks: summarizing documents (Automatic Summarization), tracking pronouns (Co-reference Resolution), analyzing multi-sentence flow (Discourse Analysis), translating languages (Machine Translation), extracting entities like names and dates (NER), converting scan images to text (OCR), and labeling parts of speech (POS Tagging).
sections.deepDive:
Core NLP Tasks (Presentation 1, Slides 24–33):
  • Automatic Summarization: Generates a concise summary preserving core information. Can be extractive (selecting verbatim sentences) or abstractive (generating novel paraphrased text).
  • Co-reference Resolution: Determining which linguistic expressions refer to the exact same real-world entity (e.g. 'Maria arrived. She sat down' → 'Maria' = 'She').
  • Discourse Analysis: Modeling relationships and argumentative structures connecting sentences.
  • Morphological Segmentation: Deconstructing polymorphemic words into their constituent roots and affixes.
  • Named Entity Recognition (NER): Locating and classifying mentions of proper entities into predefined types (Person, Organization, Location, Date).
  • Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Converting pixel data from scanned documents into machine-editable text (e.g. Pytesseract).
  • Part of Speech (POS) Tagging: Assigning grammatical category tags to each token in a sentence based on syntax and lexicon.

sections.title: 1.3 Morphemes, Lexemes, Paradigms & Roots
sections.simple: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit of a language (like prefixes, suffixes, or roots). A lexeme is an abstract dictionary word (like SING). A paradigm is the entire family of forms realizing that lexeme ({sing, sang, sung, sings, singing}). The root is the core base morpheme before adding any affixes.
sections.deepDive:
Formal Morphological Units (Spencer & Zwicky, 1998; Presentation 2, Slides 7–10):
  • Morpheme: The minimal distinctive unit of grammar and meaning. Subdivided into:
    • Free Morphemes: Can stand alone as independent words (e.g. dog, hoe, buhay).
    • Bound Morphemes: Must attach to another morpheme (affixes like -ing, un-, -an, nag-).
    • Lexical Morphemes: Content words with referential meaning (nouns, verbs, adjectives).
    • Functional Morphemes: Grammatical glue words (prepositions, conjunctions, articles).
  • Lexeme: An abstract unit of morphological analysis corresponding to a set of word forms sharing core semantics and grammatical category (conventionally capitalized, e.g. RUN).
  • Paradigm: The complete set of word forms realizing a particular lexeme (e.g., the paradigm of SING is {cantare', sing, sang, sung, sings, singing}).
  • Root (Lexeme's Root): The fundamental base morpheme from which a paradigm of phonological words is deduced.

sections.title: 1.4 Derivation vs. Inflection & The Closure Principle
sections.simple:
Inflection modifies a word's grammar (like tense or plural) without changing its part of speech or core meaning (talk → talked; both are verbs). Derivation creates a new word or changes its part of speech (noun malice → adjective malicious).

Closure Principle: Inflection shuts the door! Once an inflectional suffix attaches, you cannot add further derivational affixes.
sections.deepDive:
Comprehensive Distinction (Presentation 2, Slides 12–15):
DimensionInflectionDerivation
Part of Speech ChangeNever changes POS (Verb → Verb: fear → fears, talk → talked)Frequently changes POS (Noun → Adj: malice → malicious; Verb → Noun: sing → singer)
Semantic MeaningPreserves core concept; modifies grammatical features (tense, aspect, number)Produces a novel semantic concept or dictionary entry
ProductivityHighly regular and productive across grammatical paradigmsVariable productivity; often semantically idiosyncratic
Affix PositionAttaches at the outer perimeter of the wordAttaches closer to the root morpheme

The Closure Principle in Morphology:
'Inflection closes words for further derivation, while derivation does not.' (Presentation 2, Slide 15). Derivational affixes must attach first; once inflectional affixes attach to mark agreement/tense, the word is closed to subsequent derivational processes (e.g. nation → national [derivation] → nationalize [derivation] → nationalized [inflection]; *nationalized-tion is ungrammatical).

sections.title: 1.5 Incorporation, Clitics & Compounding
sections.simple:
Incorporation: Fusing a verb with an object or pronoun into a single word (Kankanaey kinanko = 'ate' + 'I' → 'I ate it').
Clitics: Words that cannot stand on their own phonologically and must lean onto neighbor words (like 'm in I'm or Filipino ba, na, pa, din).
Compounding: Putting two whole words together to mean one thing (like Green House, or Kankanaey taltalak = 'toy car').
sections.deepDive:
Phenomena & Case Studies (Presentation 2, Slides 16–18):
  • Incorporation: The syntactic concatenation of a verb head with another constituent (nominal argument, pronoun, or adverb) to form a single complex predicate realizing combined grammatical relations (Gerdts, 1998).
    Kankanaey Examples:
    • kinanko = kinan (ate) + ko (I) → 'I ate it'.
    • edwani = ed (in) + nuwani (present) → 'in the present time' (showing elision of the 'nu' syllable).
  • Clitics ('Enclitics'): Syntactically independent words that lack phonological stress and therefore attach phonologically to an adjacent host word.
    English Examples: 'm in I'm, 's in he's, n't in don't/can't.
    Philippine Enclitics: Second-position discourse particles such as ba, na, pa, man, din, daw.
  • Compounding: Combination of two or more independent lexical roots into a single compound lexeme with unified semantic interpretation.
    English Example: Green House (a building for plants, not merely a house that is green).
    Kankanaey Example: From root talak (car), partial reduplication forms taltalak (toy car / miniature vehicle).

sections.title: 1.6 Kankanaey Morphology Case Study (Miguel 2009)
sections.simple: In indigenous Philippine languages like Kankanaey (Benguet), single root words act as giant semantic toolboxes! For example, the root word gabyon (a farming hoe) generates over 50 distinct inflected, derived, and incorporated words, and ali (to come) generates complex tenses, companions, and actions.
sections.deepDive:
Research Reference: Morphology Primer of the Kankanaey Language of Benguet Philippines (Dalos Miguel, 2009). Nouns and verbs in Kankanaey serve as semantic repositories producing dozens of derivations, inflections, and compound incorporations.

Key Affixation Phenomena:
  • Prefixation: Adding morpheme before root (e.g. igabyon → will use the hoe).
  • Suffixation: Adding morpheme after root (e.g. gabyonan → to use a hoe to dig an area).
  • Infixation: Inserting morpheme inside root (e.g. g-in-abyon → hoe was used; g-um-abyon → will use a hoe).
  • Reduplication: Repeating root syllables (e.g. gab-gabyon → miniature/toy hoe; ginabgabyon).
  • Compound Incorporation: Concatenating roots and pronouns: mangabyonda ('they will use a hoe'), nangabyonak ('I used a hoe'), gabyonko ('my hoe').
The Paradigm of 'ali' (to come):
  • inmali (Verb-simple past): came
  • inmal-ali (Verb-past perfect): had come
  • inmaliali (Verb-past continuous): had always been coming
  • kaal-ali (Adjective): referring to an object who came recently
  • kaali (Adjective): referring to an object who came immediately
  • umal-ali (Verb-present continuous): coming
  • umaliak (Verb + pronoun): I come / I will come
  • makiali (Verb-simple future): will come as a companion
  • kaanali (Adjective): referring to objects who suddenly came

sections.title: 1.7 POS Tagging Approaches & Tagsets
sections.simple: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging labels words as nouns, verbs, adjectives, etc. It can be Supervised (learns from human-labeled text) or Unsupervised (clusters untagged text automatically). It can use grammar rules (Rule-Based) or statistical chances (Probabilistic / HMM). In Tagalog, Rabo created a 59-tag set and Dr. Buban expanded it to 65 tags.
sections.deepDive:
POS Tagging Architectures:
  • Supervised Tagging: Utilizes a pre-annotated training corpus annotated by expert linguists. Extracts word frequencies, affix patterns, and tag n-gram transition probabilities.
  • Unsupervised Tagging: Induces tag sets and dictionary clusters directly from raw untagged corpora using clustering algorithms (e.g. Expectation-Maximization, Baum-Welch).
  • Rule-Based POS Tagging: Leverages human-crafted linguistic rule databases (e.g. Eric Brill's Transformation-Based Tagger). Rule example: 'If a word is preceded by a determiner (DTC) and followed by a noun (NNC), tag it as an adjective (JJD).'
  • Probabilistic POS Tagging (Hidden Markov Models - HMM): Finds optimal tag sequence $\hat{T} = \arg\max_T P(T|W) = \arg\max_T P(T)P(W|T)$. Employs the Markov Assumption where the probability of tag $t_i$ depends only on preceding tag $t_{i-1}$ (Bigram) or $t_{i-2}, t_{i-1}$ (Trigram). Combines:
    • Lexical / Emission Probability: $P(w_i | t_i)$ — probability of word $w$ given tag $t$.
    • Contextual / Transition Probability: $P(t_i | t_{i-1})$ — probability of tag $t_i$ following tag $t_{i-1}$.
Standard Tagsets:
  • Tagalog Tagsets: Rabo (2004) Tagset = 59 tags; Revised Tagalog Tagset by Dr. Buban = 65 tags.
  • English Tagsets: Penn Treebank (NN, NNS, NNP, NNPS, PRP, VB, VBD, JJ, RB); CLAWS Tagset (NN1, NN2, VVO, AJO); Universal Tagset.
  • Tag Distribution in Tagalog Corpora: NNC (Common Noun) is the highest frequency tag and the most common default tag assigned to unknown words. VBOI has zero/lowest frequency.
  • Corpus Validity Factors: Punctuation delimiters (. , ! ?), double quotes, ellipses, and ambiguous abbreviations with periods (e.g. 'Dr.', 'e.g.') which confound sentence boundary detection.

sections.title: 1.8 Foundational Architecture: 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017)
sections.simple: The Transformer revolutionized NLP by getting rid of slow step-by-step loops (RNNs/LSTMs) and convolutions completely! Instead, it connects every word in a sentence to every other word simultaneously using Self-Attention. This allows massive parallel training on GPUs and powers modern NLP models like BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT.
sections.deepDive:
Seminal Architecture (Vaswani et al., NIPS 2017):

Core Equations & Components:
  • Scaled Dot-Product Attention:$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$Where $Q$ (Query), $K$ (Key), and $V$ (Value) are vector matrices. The scaling factor $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ is essential: for large dimensions $d_k$, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ stabilizes gradient flow.
  • Multi-Head Attention:$$\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)W^O$$$$\text{where } \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)$$Employs $h = 8$ parallel attention heads with $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h = 512/8 = 64$. Allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.
  • Encoder & Decoder Stacks: Both consist of stacks of $N = 6$ identical layers:
    • Encoder (2 sub-layers): Multi-Head Self-Attention + Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN). Each sub-layer uses residual connections followed by Layer Normalization: $\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))$. Model dimension $d_{model} = 512$.
    • Decoder (3 sub-layers): Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (masks future positions $-\infty$ to enforce autoregressive property) + Encoder-Decoder Cross-Attention (Queries from decoder, Keys/Values from encoder) + Position-wise FFN.
  • Position-wise Feed-Forward Network:$$\text{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$$Inner layer dimension $d_{ff} = 2048$, with ReLU activation.
  • Sinusoidal Positional Encoding: Injects sequence order without recurrence:$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}}), \quad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}})$$
  • Computational Complexity Advantage: Self-attention layer connects all positions with $O(1)$ sequential operations and path length $O(1)$, compared to $O(n)$ sequential operations in recurrent layers (RNNs).
  • Benchmark Results: Established state-of-the-art on WMT 2014 English-to-German (28.4 BLEU) and English-to-French (41.8 BLEU), trained in just 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs.

sections.title: 1.9 Evaluation Metrics in NLP
sections.simple: NLP models are evaluated using standard metrics: Accuracy (total correct divided by total), Precision (when it predicts a tag, how often is it right?), Recall (how many of the actual targets did it find?), and F1-Score (the harmonic mean balancing Precision and Recall). Error Rate is simply $1 - \text{Accuracy}$. BLEU evaluates machine translation.
sections.deepDive:
Mathematical Formulations:
  • Accuracy: $\frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} = \frac{\text{Correct Predictions}}{\text{Total Predictions}}$
  • Precision: $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ — Measures quality and absence of false alarms.
  • Recall (Sensitivity): $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ — Measures completeness and absence of missed targets.
  • F1-Measure: $2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$ — Harmonic mean penalizing extreme imbalances.
  • Error Rate: $1 - \text{Accuracy} = \frac{FP + FN}{\text{Total}}$
  • BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy): Geometric mean of modified n-gram precisions multiplied by a brevity penalty, used specifically for evaluating Machine Translation quality.

modules.title: Domain 2: Studies on NLP Presented by Class Groups
modules.summary: Covers all 8 academic research papers from Saint Louis University presented by class groups in CSE 30, with deep coverage of Group 2 (RoBERTa SDG), Group 4 (InfoSentiA), Group 5 (Baguio BERTopic + VADER), and Groups 1, 3, 6, 7, 8.

sections.title: 2.1 Group 2: Cloud-Based RoBERTa for Academic Institutions' SDG Contributions
sections.simple:
Problem: Universities produce tons of sustainability reports, but evaluating them by hand is slow, biased, and risks 'SDG-washing' (fake green claims). Existing tools like STARS only give broad ratings and cannot map text to the 17 individual UN SDGs.
Solution: A cloud web app on Google Cloud (Vertex AI + Firestore) fine-tuning RoBERTa with TF-IDF, NLTK, and LexDG (a dictionary of regional Ilocano/Philippine words). Achieved 96.77% accuracy (0.74 F1), beating standard BERT and SVM. Taking away LexDG dropped F1 to 0.68!
sections.deepDive:
Full Paper Details: Dalos Miguel, Jahn Crystan Abella et al. / Group 2 (Baladad, Cardenas, Domalanta, Javier, Menos, Sanchez), SLU 2026. Presented at IEEE ISCI.

Key Architecture & Results:
  • Dataset: 748 documents across 15 Philippine HEIs collected via Selenium/BeautifulSoup web scraping and Pytesseract OCR for scanned PDFs. Multi-hot vector encoding for 17 SDGs.
  • Preprocessing: NLTK tokenization, POS-assisted lemmatization, stopword removal, random oversampling for class imbalance. Split: 80% train / 10% val / 10% test.
  • LexDG: Custom domain-specific lexicon of Philippine regional terms (Ilocano) to prevent misclassification of localized phrasing.
  • BERT vs. RoBERTa Matrix: RoBERTa uses dynamic masking (vs. static), removes Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), trains on 160 GB data (vs. 16 GB), uses Byte-level BPE 50k vocab (vs. WordPiece 30k), and scales batch sizes up to 8,000.
  • Results: 96.77% Weighted Accuracy, 0.80 Micro-Precision, 0.70 Micro-Recall, 0.74 Micro-F1. Outperformed Logistic Regression (0.64 F1), SVM (0.67 F1), and BERT (0.70 F1).
  • Ablation Study: Removing LexDG dropped F1 from 0.74 to 0.68.
  • Deployment: Google Cloud Platform (Vertex AI, Firestore, Flask API, Node.js frontend), estimated at ₱2,700–₱8,300/month.
  • Limitations: Category overlap between SDG 2 (Zero Hunger, lowest F1 0.55) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) due to shared agricultural keywords. Highest F1 was SDG 7 (Clean Energy, 0.95 F1).

sections.title: 2.2 Group 5: Extracting Topics & Sentiments from Baguio City Social Media Using BERTopic & VADER
sections.simple:
Problem: Social media comments about Baguio City (tourism, traffic, weather, ordinances) are written in a mix of English, Tagalog, and Ilocano. Previous studies translated everything to English first, which ruined cultural slang and context!
Solution: Group 5 combined BERTopic (to find the top discussion topics without translation) and a customized dual-language VADER sentiment tool with 123 degree words (like sobra, medyo) and contrast words (like Tagalog pero, Ilocano ngem). Achieved 72.74% binary accuracy (0.7734 F1) on 500 hand-labeled comments.
sections.deepDive:
Full Paper Details: Lance Gabrielle Arevalo, Christian Gabriel Bayquen, Arian Carl Cayton, Jp De los Trinos, Jaime Fernandez (SLU SAMCIS, ICITE 2023).

Methodology & Pipeline:
  • Data Sources: Comments gathered via web scraping from Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, YouTube, and Reddit regarding Baguio City tourism, living, and governance.
  • Word-Lexicon Dataset: Merged Tagalog & Ilocano words from R's Tidytext sentiment package and Kaggle 81-language sentiment lexicons, mapped to English VADER polarity scores (-1 to +1).
  • BERTopic Topic Modeling: Preprocessing via tokenization, stopword removal, lowercasing. Embeddings from BERT clustered with class-based TF-IDF (c-TF-IDF). Uses Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) with diversity value 0.8 to prevent duplicate/plural keywords. Reduced 200–300 raw topics to 100 via reduce_topics(), then merged into 15 governance topics (Outlier 52%, Tourism 16%, Arts/Culture 10%, Infrastructure 8%, Parks & Rec 8%, Public Safety 8%, Public Transport 6%, Food 4%, Housing 3%, Community Dev 2%, Healthcare 1%, Environment 1%). Coherence score: 0.4043 for 9 predefined topics.
  • VADER Sentiment Heuristics (5 Rules Adapted):
    1. Capitalization: ALL CAPS receives higher emotional weight ('I AM VERY HAPPY' > 'I am very happy').
    2. Punctuation: Amplifies score for multiple exclamation/question marks ('I like it!!!' > 'I like it.').
    3. Degree Modifiers (123 words): Adverbs of manner (pang-abay na pamaraan) that intensify (Tagalog sobra, napaka, malaki) or weaken (medyo, bahagya) sentiment.
    4. Shift in Polarity Due to 'But': Initial clause overridden by contrasting conjunctions: Tagalog pero, ngunit, subalit, bagkus; Ilocano ngem (e.g. 'Mahal kita, pero ayaw na kitang makasama' → negative dominates).
    5. Negation (62 words): Inverting polarity when negation particles appear (e.g. Tagalog hindi, huwag, English not, never; e.g. 'Hindi ka matinong kausap').
  • Experimental Results on 500 Annotations:
    • Binary Classification: Accuracy: 72.74%, Precision: 0.8700, Recall: 0.7274, F1-Score: 0.7734 (MAE: Positive 45.25, Negative 6.94; RMSE: Pos 63.82, Neg 20.61).
    • Multiclass Classification (Pos, Neg, Neutral): Accuracy: 55.98%, Precision: 0.6698, F1-Score: 0.5822. Model struggled with neutrality because human annotators tended to score slightly positive comments as neutral.

sections.title: 2.3 Group 4: InfoSentiA: Local Legislation System with Sentiment Analysis Feedback
sections.simple:
Problem: The Baguio City Council (Sangguniang Panlungsod) struggled to gather citizen feedback on newly passed laws and ordinances because manual paper questionnaires were too slow and had low response rates.
Solution: An e-governance portal called InfoSentiA that automatically posts city ordinances to Facebook using the Facebook Graph API, collects citizen comments, and feeds them into Project Lengua, an AFINN-based sentiment API (-5 to +5 scores). It draws live donut charts ('Ordinance Pulse') for city officials to see if the public supports or opposes a law.
sections.deepDive:
Full Paper Details: Christopher Edrian Espiritu, Mark Joshua Eslao, Dean Earl Donglawen, Charlene Fama, Jay Garcia, Sean Dustine Genove, Mary Anne Zheng, Mary Jane Zheng (SLU SAMCIS). Client: Research Division of the Sangguniang Panlungsod ng Baguio (RDSP) pursuant to RA 7160 (Local Government Code).

System Architecture & Implementation:
  • Development Model: Evolutionary Prototyping Model with client feedback loops and daily 15-minute standup meetings.
  • Two-Tier Software Architecture:
    1. Main System: Responsive web portal built on the LAMP stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP/Laravel, Bootstrap, jQuery, Vue.js), deployed on Heroku PaaS. Provides document repositories, search/indexing for watermarked ordinances/resolutions, and questionnaire management.
    2. Sub-System ('Project Lengua'): Dedicated RESTful sentiment analysis microservice built on Node.js, Express, and MongoDB, deployed on Heroku. Exposes GET/POST API endpoints at https://project-lengua.herokuapp.com/api.
  • Sentiment Analysis Engine: Supervised text classification using the AFINN lexicon (Nielsen, 2011), rating words on a scale from -5 (extremely negative) to +5 (extremely positive). API accepts word, dialect, and score parameters.
  • Facebook Graph API Integration: When the RDSP admin uploads an approved city resolution, InfoSentiA automatically cross-posts it to the official Baguio City Facebook page. It then pulls citizen replies and comments for batch processing through Project Lengua.
  • Outputs: Real-time sentiment distribution visualized as donut charts ('Ordinance Pulse') showing positive, negative, and neutral shares, with downloadable XLS statistical reports to guide legislative amendments or repeals.

sections.title: 2.4 Group 1: Language Mapping of the Cordillera (CAR) Using Relational Model
sections.simple: Summary: Group 1 mapped out the diverse indigenous languages of the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR) to specific towns and provinces using a relational database model with PSA data and native speaker translations. They identified 22 distinct indigenous languages across CAR and built a web prototype to preserve regional cultural heritage.
sections.deepDive:
Paper: Dalos D. Miguel, John Austin T. Andres, Heidi F. Batara et al. (IJCSR 2024).
Maps CAR languages (Benguet, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Kalinga, Apayao, Abra) to avoid language barriers and preserve indigenous heritage. Connected to Presentation 1, Slides 68–72.

sections.title: 2.5 Group 3: Bi-directional Ilocano-English Translator Using Customized Moses SMT
sections.simple: Summary: Group 3 built an automated two-way translator between Ilocano and English using the open-source Moses Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) system with bilingual sentence pairs, GIZA++ word alignment, and n-gram language models.
sections.deepDive:
Paper: Dalos D. Miguel, J. Bautista, C. Bayla, K. Fianza et al. (NNLPRS 2015).
Customized Moses phrase-based statistical machine translation system using parallel bi-text corpora. Demonstrated that SMT can effectively translate low-resource Philippine regional languages without needing manual parsers.

sections.title: 2.6 Group 6: LexiLoko 2.0: Lexicon-Integrated NMT for Iloko Preservation
sections.simple: Summary: Group 6 digitized phased-out Mother Tongue (MTB-MLE) modules from DepEd-Pangasinan (4,065 words and 1,833 sentence pairs) to train a Transformer Neural Machine Translation model for Ilocano, using a 'lexicon-pointer' to fix rare-word translation errors.
sections.deepDive:
Paper: Hannah Ragudos, Marius Glenn Nonato, Stephen Coloma, Leonhard Leung et al. (SLU SAMCIS).
Integrates a bilingual Iloko-English dictionary with pretrained Transformer NMT. The custom 'lexicon-pointer' mechanism dynamically looks up rare and out-of-vocabulary words during decoding to preserve endangered regional language vocabulary.

sections.title: 2.7 Group 7: Comparative Evaluation of Tagalog Part-of-Speech Taggers
sections.simple: Summary: Tested 4 different Tagalog POS taggers to see which works best on unseen text. PTPOST4.1 (Hidden Markov Model) won with 78.3% accuracy on unseen test data, while MBPOST (Memory-based) did best (85.0%) on familiar training data. (This is the source of Slide 55 in Presentation 1!).
sections.deepDive:
Paper: Dalos D. Miguel and Rachel Edita O. Roxas (NNLPRS 2007).
Evaluated 4 taggers: PTPOST4.1 (Probabilistic HMM with Viterbi), MBPOST (Memory-based), Tag-Alog (Rule-based), and TPOST (Template-based n-gram). Established that probabilistic HMM models generalize best to unseen Tagalog text.

sections.title: 2.8 Group 8: Modeling Kankanaey Adjective Inflections
sections.simple: Summary: Modeled how the indigenous Kankanaey language forms adjectives using prefixes, suffixes, infixes (like -in-, -um-), and word repetitions (reduplication like talak → taltalak). Proved that indigenous languages follow regular rules that computers can parse. (Forms the basis of Presentation 2!).
sections.deepDive:
Paper: Dalos D. Miguel (SLU, NNLPRS 2009).
Formalized computational morphological rules for Kankanaey affixes, including semantic repositories like gabyon (50+ words) and adjective intensity/habitual aspect derivations.

modules.title: Domain 3: Bag of Words & Naive Bayes Classification
modules.summary: Covers Bag of Words vectorization, the Panatang Makabayan 44 to 37 dimensionality reduction exercise, vector inversion, Conditional Probability, Naive Bayes derivation, denominator cancellation proof, Laplace +1 smoothing, and language identification.

sections.title: 3.1 Bag of Words (BoW) Mechanics & Vector Space
sections.simple: Bag of Words (BoW) turns text into lists of numbers (vectors). It counts how many times each vocabulary word appears in a text while throwing away sentence grammar and word order (like throwing words into a bag).
sections.deepDive:
Technical Formulation: BoW maps text documents into a fixed-length numeric vector space $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$, where $|V|$ is the size of the vocabulary.

Steps:
  1. Normalization: Lowercasing and tokenization.
  2. Vocabulary Construction: Unique words indexed alphabetically from $1$ to $|V|$.
  3. Vectorization: For document $D$, vector $\vec{v} = [c_1, c_2, \dots, c_{|V|}]$ where $c_i$ is the count of word $w_i$.
  4. Limitations: Discards word order, ignores grammar, produces sparse vectors, and suffers from the curse of dimensionality.

sections.title: 3.2 The SLU Panatang Makabayan BoW Case Study
sections.simple: In our class exercise, we took the Panatang Makabayan text and built a 44-word vocabulary. Then we removed 7 stopwords (ang, at, ko, mga, nang, ng, sa), reducing the vocabulary down to 37 words. Words are re-indexed alphabetically, with aking at Index 1 (count 4) and Pilipinas at Index 30 (count 3).
sections.deepDive:
Step-by-Step Breakdown (BagOfWordExercise.pdf):

Part 1: 44-Word Initial Vocabulary:
Derived from lowercasing the pledge (total 64 tokens across 44 unique vocabulary words).
Vector for the opening clause 'Iniibig ko ang Pilipinas':
  • Index 3 (ang): count 1
  • Index 11 (iniibig): count 1
  • Index 15 (ko): count 1

sections.title: 3.3 Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem
sections.simple: Conditional probability $P(A|B)$ is the chance of $A$ happening given that $B$ already happened: $P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Bayes' Rule lets us flip conditional probabilities: $P(C|X) = \frac{P(X|C)P(C)}{P(X)}$.
sections.deepDive:
Mathematical Definitions (Presentation 3, Slides 5–20):
$$P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$$
Worked Problem (Slides 16–18):
Out of 100 school members: 80 Students, 20 Teachers/Staff; 32 Female Students.
$$P(\text{Female} | \text{Student}) = \frac{P(\text{Female} \cap \text{Student})}{P(\text{Student})} = \frac{32/100}{80/100} = \frac{32}{80} = 0.40\text{ (or }2/5\text{)}$$
Bayes' Rule:
$$P(Y|X) = \frac{P(X|Y) \cdot P(Y)}{P(X)}$$

sections.title: 3.4 Naive Bayes Assumption & Denominator Cancellation
sections.simple:
Naive Bayes assumes all words in a sentence are completely independent of each other.

Why drop the denominator? When deciding which class wins, the denominator $P(X)$ is identical for every candidate category. Because it divides everything by the exact same number, it never changes who wins, so we discard it completely!
sections.deepDive:
Conditional Independence Assumption:
$$P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n | C) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i | C)$$
Full Formulation:
$$P(C | X_1, \dots, X_n) = \frac{P(C) \prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i | C)}{P(X_1, \dots, X_n)}$$
The Denominator Cancellation Proof (Slides 45 & 74–79):
Because the denominator $P(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ is independent of category $C$ and identical across all candidate classes, it functions as a constant scaling factor. Therefore, for the argmax decision rule, the denominator is omitted:
$$\hat{C} = \arg\max_{C \in \Gamma} \left[ P(C) \prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i | C) \right]$$

sections.title: 3.5 Language Identification & Laplace (+1) Smoothing
sections.simple: We identify whether text is Ilocano, Tagalog, or Pangasinan by multiplying word likelihoods for each language and picking the highest score. If an unseen word has a chance of 0, multiplying by 0 would wipe out the whole score! We fix this using Laplace (+1) Smoothing by adding 1 to all word counts so nothing ever equals zero.
sections.deepDive:
Multinomial Naive Bayes Language Identification (Slides 47–79):
$$\hat{L} = \arg\max_{L \in \Gamma} \left[ P(L) \prod_{i=1}^n P(w_i | L) \right]$$
Example from Slide 76:
$$P(\text{Ilocano} | \text{'naimbag', 'nga', 'rabii'}) \propto P(\text{Ilocano}) \times P(\text{'naimbag'}|\text{Ilocano}) \times P(\text{'nga'}|\text{Ilocano}) \times P(\text{'rabii'}|\text{Ilocano})$$

Laplace (+1) Smoothing:
$$P_{\text{Laplace}}(w|C) = \frac{\text{Count}(w, C) + 1}{\sum_{w'} \text{Count}(w', C) + |V|}$$Slide 66 also introduces an explicit 'Others' category with frequency count 1 to handle out-of-vocabulary words.
